content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a spatio-temporal learning framework named SimST for traffic forecasting. The core proposal is to avoid using graph neural networks for spatial correlation modelling, and hence to improve the model forecasting efficiency. To achieve this, the paper proposes to use two modules to encode the spatial correlations: a spatial position injector and a spatial proximity injector. The spatial position injector is an MLP that starts with random position encodings and uses back propagation at training to learn spatial position encodings for the nodes (e.g., sensors or locations of interest). The spatial proximity injector simply concatenates each node's traffic observation with those of its top-k neighbours. 

Experimental results on five real datasets comparing against 11 baseline methods confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The proposal to get rid of graph neural networks for spatial correlation learning in traffic forecasting is interesting and may intrigue a series of follow-up studies. 

2. Although the proposed model structure is simple, it achieves state-of-art forecasting accuracy while being much faster in model inference.

Weakness:
1. The proposal is a heuristic without performance guarantees (although most of the existing works on this topic share the same issue).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very well written and easy to follow. None of the model components are particularly new, but they are put together in a way that is shown to produce the state-of-the-art accuracy.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4rep
content.comment:
Thanks for your positive comments on our paper writing and superior model performance. We further add more clarifications corresponding to the given comments below.

[C1] The reason why such a simple model outperforms other baselines is not explained. The model only utilizes the spatial information in the Spatial Proximity Injector, but it outperforms other GNN-baselines based on not only the original matrix but also the adaptive matrix. This should be further explained.

[A1] Thanks for this comment. First, we would like to clarify that the spatial information is provided by both the spatial position injector and spatial proximity injector. Second, we apologize for not clearly stating why our method can outperform other baselines. The reasons are as follows. GNN-based models require all nodes to be involved in the message passing step, and thus the model needs to simultaneously forecast the future for every node. Since traffic forecasting is a challenging task, such joint forecasts over all nodes make it extremely difficult to optimize the model parameters. In contrast, SimST can be seen as a single-node model, which means that each node is processed individually by the model. This makes the optimization process easier. The learning curve figure in Appendix A.5 validates our hypothesis, where SimST exhibits significantly faster convergence rates than other baselines.

[C2] Adding the proposed module based on these vanilla models and showing the performance should be more convincing.

[A2] Thanks for pointing this out. Following your suggestion, we have included the vanilla models’ results in Figure 3 of the main paper. We also modified the text (in blue color) to reflect this change.

[C3] The reproducibility is not good, since the provided code is not reproducible. I run the code by default setting on PEMS-04 on 3080ti torch 1.10.0, and only get MAPE above 0.11.

[A3] We believe that this comment may be based on a misunderstanding. Actually, the results achieved by the reviewer, especially this line: "Average Test MAE: 18.7109, Test RMSE: 30.2952, Test MAPE: 0.1272" is basically the same as our reported results in the last row of Table 2 (18.68, 30.30, 12.72%). Thus, we believe that your reproduced results actually verify the reproducibility of our code. We would like you to please consider updating your score if our reproducibility is not a problem.

Thank you again for the valuable feedback. Please let us know if you have any other comments/questions.

content.title: Still confusing
content.comment:
Thank you for the detailed answers. However, A1 is not convincing to me.

1. The logic of A1 is here, "GNN-based models require all nodes to be involved in the message passing step, and thus the model needs to forecast the future for every node simultaneously." so "such joint forecasts over all nodes make it extremely difficult to optimize the model parameters". This seems illogical. One situation that this statement is true is that different nodes have different distributions. If so, the further experiment should be conducted.

2. I don't think a learning curve could demonstrate the point of the response. The parameter size also significantly influences the learning curve.

content.title: Thank you for your reply
content.comment:
Thanks for your reply. We are sorry for not making it clear, and we would like to further clarify your concern as follows.

Response to 1: actually it is true that different nodes have diverse distributions in the spatio-temporal data. This point has verified by several impactful papers [1-4]. For example in AGCRN [3] (262 citations), the authors point out that "traffic series exhibit diversified patterns, they may appear similar, dissimilar, and even contradictory owning to the distinct attributes across a variety of data sources."

[1] Matrix Factorization for Spatio-Temporal Neural Networks with Applications to Urban Flow Prediction. CIKM 2019.

[2] Urban traffic prediction from spatio-temporal data using deep meta learning. KDD 2019.

[3] Adaptive Graph Convolutional Recurrent Network for Traffic Forecasting. NeurIPS 2020.

[4] Pre-training Enhanced Spatial-temporal Graph Neural Network for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting. KDD 2022.


Response to 2: currently in the paper, the parameter size of SimST is less than the other GNN-based methods. For example, SimST-CT has 150k parameters, and GWNET has around 300k parameters. Therefore, the reviewer may attribute our faster converange rates to the size of parameters. But we have conducted experiments before on setting the parameter size of SimST-CT to 400k, which is larger than GWNET. The results show that the learning curves of SimST-CT with 150k and 400k parameters are basically the same. Thus, the parameter size will not influence our learning process much, and our proposed method still has superior convergence rates than the other baselines. By the way, since you have already run our code, the aforementioned results can be validated by changing init_dim from 64 to 128 (in the code). And then you can compare the curves with different parameter sizes.

Moreover, we would like to argue that using learning curve to empirically reflect the difficulty of learning process is a common way in the literature. For example, in the Figure 1-3 of the Adam [5] approach, the authors use the learning curve to demonstrate the supriority of the proposed method empirically.

[5] Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization. ICLR 2015.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1y45
content.comment:
Thank you very much for appreciating the novelty of the proposed idea and the quality of our presentation. We address the questions as below.

[C1] The model actually utilizes the adjacency information and the spatial proximity injector works the same way as graph convolution. The whole framework is not that GNN-free.

[A1] Sincere thanks for raising this concern. We would like to clarify it as follows. The core component of GNNs is the message passing step, where features are aggregated to the anchor node via a weighted summation operation. And typically, a stack of GNN layers are required to propagate the information. In contrast, our spatial proximity injector only concatenates the raw time series data from neighbors to the anchor node. We do not need the process of feature aggregation (or weighted sum). Thus, we argue that it would be safe to say that our framework is GNN-free.

[C2] In the paragraph under Eq(4), the author says ‘Note that this injector operates in the data preprocessing stage, so it has no influence on model training and inference.’ It seems that the time consumption of Spatial Proximity Injector is not taken into consideration while comparing efficiency, which could be unfair for baselines.

[A2] Thanks for pointing this out. In fact, some baselines also require data preprocessing. For example, STGODE requires the construction of a semantic adjacency matrix by using the dynamic time warping algorithm to precompute the similarity of two time series. We do not count its cost in this stage either. Moreover, we would like to argue that it is common practice in the community to only compare efficiency during training and inference. For example, GWNET compares the training and inference time per epoch with baselines in Table 4 of its paper. AGCRN compares the training time per epoch in Table 3 of its main paper. Lastly, we would like to provide you with the preprocessing time. The time are around 40.3 seconds and 248.7 seconds on the PeMSD4 and LA datasets, respectively. Considering that the preprocessed inputs can be stored and reused, we think that the cost of a few minutes could be cheap.

[C3] Since the motivation of the work falls on efficiency, the author should compare more metrics. TPS is not as straightforward as training and inferring time per epoch.

[A3] Thanks for your advice. We have attached the details of the training and inference time per epoch in Appendix A.3. We also modified the main paper (in blue text) to point out this change. For the inference efficiency, the conclusions of using inferring time are similar to that of using TPS. For the training time, SimST variants are generally slower than GWN and AGCRN, due to the usage of a small actual batch size.

Thank you again for the valuable feedback. Please let us know if you have any other comments/questions.

content.title: Response to Reviewer k8Ws
content.comment:
[C1] The proposed approach’s main contribution is to add spatial information as new features through manual processing. No new machine learning model/algorithms are proposed. The contribution of the paper is very limited.

[A1] We respectfully disagree with the reviewer. Our contributions go significantly beyond adding spatial information as new features. We have listed our three contributions at the end of the introduction section, but their full depth bears further emphasis.

Thus, we would like to clarify our contributions. Most existing STGNNs approaches rely on GNNs to model spatial dependencies, leading to high computational cost and poor scalability. In our work, we demonstrate that it is feasible to remove GNNs from traffic forecasting tasks altogether and replace them with our new SimST framework design. The SimST framework confirms that GNNs are unnecessary for spatial modeling in traffic forecasting. Our approach achieves two significant benefits: with almost always better accuracy, and several times faster inference speed (e.g., SimST-WN is 11× - 17× and 30× - 39× faster than STGODE and STGNCDE, respectively.)

Moreover, we believe that simplicity is not in itself a flaw: simple methods are more easily adopted and built upon, which is an important contributor to research progress and impact. In the computer vision and graph domains, MLP-Mixer [1], SGC [2] and GLNN [3] showed that simple MLP or MLP-like architectures achieved competitive performance to conventional architectures, and were influential in questioning conventional wisdom and sparking further research into more diverse architectures.

[1] MLP-Mixer: An all-MLP Architecture for Vision. NeurIPS 2021. [2] Simplifying Graph Convolutional Networks. ICML 2019. [3] Graph-Less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation. ICLR 2022

[C2] The evaluation results show very marginal improvements over existing approaches. No statistical significance provided.

[A2] Thanks for raising this concern. However, we believe that SimST’s performance improvements are not marginal, but rather substantial. For example, in Table 2 of the main paper, we can see that the earlier STGODE improves the performance from 21.19 (achieved by STSGCN) to 20.84 on the PeMSD4 dataset (a 1.7% improvement) while GMSDR further enhances the performance to 20.49 (also a 1.7% improvement). Both STGODE and GMSDR were published at top-tier conferences, i.e., KDD. Compared to the latest papers GMSDR and STGNCDE in this year, our method advances the result from 20.49/19.21 to 18.68 (a 8.8/2.8% improvement). Thus, we argue that our method achieves a significant performance gain over existing arts.

This result is even more compelling considering that the goal of our SimST method is to show that a GNN-free model can be competitive. Thus, we achieved beyond expectations that the performance is not only competitive, but actually beats existing methods. In terms of statistical significance, we performed the corresponding tests, as mentioned in the caption of Table 2.


[C3] The way the adjacency matrix is defined lacks generalizability.

[A3] In fact, using road network distance to describe the proximity between nodes is the mainstream method in the traffic forecasting research field. For example, DCRNN (a pioneering work in traffic forecasting) defines the adjacency matrix based on the road network distance. Many follow-ups (including ours) use the same matrix definition as DCRNN, e.g., STGCN, GWNET, STSGCN, STGODE, and so on. Thus, it is common practice to define the matrix based on the road network distance.

Thank you again for the valuable feedback. Please let us know if you have any other comments/question
